planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Trousseau is a tall Division 1 trumpet daffodil bred by Oregon hybridizer Grant Mitsch, with a creamy perianth and a long trumpet that opens pale yellow and matures to apricot-pink.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Trousseau is a Division 1 trumpet daffodil bred by Pacific Northwest hybridizer Grant Mitsch, bearing a smooth ivory-cream perianth around a long, elegantly flared trumpet that opens soft lemon-yellow and warms to a muted apricot-pink as it ages, particularly in cool weather. It flowers on tall, sturdy stems in mid-season and has long been valued by collectors for the subtlety of its pink tone compared with brighter modern pink trumpets. Like most trumpet daffodils, Trousseau needs a real winter chill to rebloom reliably and is best treated as a fall-planted, spring-discarded display bulb rather than a perennializer in the warm Gulf Coast South. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply where winters are cold enough.

common_name: Las Vegas Daffodil (Large White-and-Yellow Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Las Vegas is a popular modern Dutch-bred trumpet daffodil with a broad white perianth and a long, butter-yellow trumpet.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Las Vegas is a Division 1 trumpet daffodil of modern Dutch breeding, producing very large flowers with broad, overlapping white perianth segments surrounding a long, trumpet of rich butter-yellow that widens and ruffles slightly at the mouth. Its exceptional flower size and strong, weather-resistant stems have made it one of the most widely distributed trumpet daffodils in the retail bulb trade in recent decades. As with most Division 1 trumpets, it needs a sustained winter chill to flower well in subsequent years, so gardeners in mild-winter areas such as the Gulf Coast should expect it to perform mainly as a one-season display bulb rather than a long-term perennial. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed where climate allows them to persist.

common_name: Loch Hope Daffodil (Giant Late Golden Large-Cupped Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Loch Hope is a British-bred large-cupped daffodil noted for producing some of the largest flowers of any daffodil cultivar, with a deep golden perianth and a wide, ruffled cup of matching color.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Loch Hope is a Division 2 large-cupped daffodil bred by British hybridizer John Lea, carrying some of the largest flowers found in the genus, with broad, deep golden-yellow perianth segments surrounding a wide, heavily ruffled cup of similar rich gold. It blooms later than most large-cupped cultivars, extending the daffodil season on tall, sturdy stems that stand up well in exhibition and garden settings alike. Its sheer flower size and clean, uniform color have kept it a favorite on the show bench for decades. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over time.

common_name: Romance Daffodil (White Large-Cupped Daffodil with Rose-Pink Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Romance is a Dutch-bred large-cupped daffodil with a clean white perianth and a cup that opens pale apricot and deepens to a soft rose-pink.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Romance is a Division 2 large-cupped daffodil of Dutch breeding, bearing broad, rounded white perianth segments around a smooth cup that opens soft apricot and warms to a dusky rose-pink as the bloom matures and is exposed to sunlight. It belongs to the same general lineage of pink-cupped large-cups as Passionale and Precocious, and is grown for the same clean color contrast and sturdy, mid-season stems. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over time.

common_name: Sinopel Daffodil (White Small-Cupped Daffodil with Green Eye)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Sinopel is a Grant Mitsch-bred small-cupped daffodil notable for the unusual green coloring at the base of its cup, a trait he used to found a whole line of green-eyed cultivars.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Sinopel is a Division 3 small-cupped daffodil bred by Oregon hybridizer Grant Mitsch, with a clean white perianth surrounding a small, flat cup that is pale yellow-green shading to a distinct olive-green base, an unusual color rarely seen in daffodils. It was one of the foundational green-eyed cultivars behind a later line of green-centered breeding, and it remains sought after by collectors for its distinctive, almost otherworldly color combination. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply slowly over time.

common_name: Verona Daffodil (White Small-Cupped Daffodil with Pale Cream Cup)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Verona is an early-to-mid twentieth-century Dutch-bred small-cupped daffodil with a pure white perianth and a neat, pale creamy-yellow cup.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in fall. Verona is a Division 3 small-cupped daffodil of Dutch origin dating to the early-to-mid twentieth century, bearing a pure white perianth around a small, neat, flat-faced cup of pale cream to soft yellow that gives the flower a quiet, refined look next to bolder large-cupped and bicolor cultivars. It flowers in mid-season on medium-height stems and has long been grown as a dependable garden and cutting variety. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over time.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Pencrebar is a long-cultivated miniature double jonquil of English origin, grown for generations in Cornish gardens before wider distribution as a heirloom bulb.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun in fall. Pencrebar is a miniature double daffodil of jonquil parentage, placed in Division 4, bearing small, fully double, deep golden-yellow flowers with a strong, sweet jonquil fragrance on short, wiry stems. It has been grown in English cottage gardens for generations and, because of its jonquil heritage, it tolerates heat and summer dryness considerably better than most double trumpet-type daffodils, making it one of the more promising double daffodils for mild-winter, Gulf Coast-type climates where many standard doubles decline after a year or two. Allow foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.

common_name: Acropolis Daffodil (Fragrant White Double Poet's Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Acropolis is a double daffodil bred by American hybridizer William Pannill, with narrow, pure white double segments and the sweet fragrance typical of poeticus-derived doubles.

directions: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Acropolis is a Division 4 double daffodil bred by American hybridizer William Pannill, with numerous narrow, pure white petal segments arranged in a dense double rosette and a sweet fragrance reminiscent of its poeticus ancestry. It blooms in mid-to-late season on sturdy stems and has been valued by collectors and show growers for the crisp whiteness and symmetry of its double form, which holds up better in wind and rain than many older doubles. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply over time.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Beryl is an early twentieth-century English heirloom miniature daffodil with reflexed pale-yellow petals and a small cup that opens deep yellow and matures to orange.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Beryl is one of the earliest-raised Cyclamineus-type (Division 6) daffodils still in cultivation, a diminutive English heirloom with narrow, swept-back pale-yellow petals surrounding a small cup that opens rich golden-yellow and deepens to orange-tinged tones as it matures, carried on short stems that emerge among the first daffodils to bloom each year. Over a century in cultivation, it remains popular with collectors of historic miniatures for its distinctive two-tone coloring and dainty scale, which suits rock gardens, troughs, and the front of borders. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Lintie is a Grant Mitsch-bred jonquil hybrid with deep yellow petals and a small cup edged in contrasting orange-red, a reliable Southern-naturalizing daffodil.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun in fall. Lintie is a Division 7 Jonquilla daffodil bred by Oregon hybridizer Grant Mitsch, bearing one to three fragrant flowers per stem with bright golden-yellow perianth segments and a small, flat cup edged in a contrasting orange-red band. Like most jonquil hybrids it carries narrow, rush-like foliage and a relatively low chilling requirement, which lets it rebloom and slowly naturalize in warmer gardens, including much of the Gulf Coast South, where standard trumpet and large-cupped daffodils typically fail to return after the first year. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Scilly White is an old fragrant white tazetta long grown on England's Isles of Scilly for the cut-flower trade and, separately, passed down for generations as a heat-tolerant heirloom in old Southern U.S. gardens.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun in fall, ideally in a mild-winter climate. Scilly White is a heirloom tazetta (Division 8) daffodil bearing clusters of small, intensely fragrant, pure white flowers with a shallow cream-to-white cup, historically grown on England's Isles of Scilly for the early cut-flower trade and, quite separately, long naturalized as a reliable pass-along bulb in old homesites and cemeteries across the warm-winter American South. Unlike trumpet and large-cupped daffodils, it needs little to no winter chill and tolerates hot, humid summers well, making it one of the more dependable perennializing daffodils for Gulf Coast gardens in zone 8 and warmer. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply into dense, fragrant drifts over the years.

common_name: Dolly Mollinger Daffodil (White Split-Corona Daffodil with Orange-Yellow Frill)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Dolly Mollinger is a widely grown Dutch split-corona daffodil with a white perianth and a heavily frilled corona that opens yellow at the base and deepens to orange at the ruffled edge.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Dolly Mollinger belongs to the split-corona group (Division 11, "collar" daffodils), with a broad white perianth surrounding a corona split into irregular, heavily ruffled segments that lie nearly flat and shade from yellow near the throat to a warm orange at the frilled margin, giving the bloom a frilly, orchid-like appearance. It is one of the most widely distributed split-corona cultivars in the retail bulb trade, popular for both garden display and cut-flower arrangements because of its unusual, long-lasting form. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom without braiding or cutting it, and leave established clumps undisturbed to multiply.
